baselineConflict.$comment: Shown on a step whose baseline source policy a review found self-contradictory (roadmap/baselineConflict.ts): one entry per reviewed source, named by that record, so the words follow the source policy and not a goal.
baselineConflict.adminPortalNonAdminScope:
The baseline says this policy should block non-admins from admin portals. But the policy it actually defines targets All users and excludes no administrator — by role, account, or group. If IAMAI followed the policy definition literally, it would lock every administrator out of the admin portals. If it followed the documentation, it would need exclusions the policy doesn't have.

IAMAI won't write instructions for either interpretation because one locks admins out and the other is incomplete. Nothing is wrong in your tenant. This step waits for the baseline author to publish a corrected version. The rest of the plan is unaffected.

The campaign prepares people the scan has seen sign in. deviceBriefing.intune: Intune capability: {state}. A licence does not prove enrollment, compliance policies or app protection are configured.
details: Intune enrollment lets the organisation manage a device. Enrollment alone does not make it compliant: configure compliance policies, assign them and confirm the device reports compliant before requiring compliance.

App protection protects work data in supported iOS and Android apps, including on unenrolled phones. It requires the appropriate Intune app protection policies and supported apps. It does not manage the whole phone or cover every browser and application.

Keeping company data off phones requires an access restriction that blocks those platforms. Excluding phones from a compliant-device policy does not block them. Verify that restriction separately before treating this choice as implemented.

Microsoft Entra hybrid join connects an on-premises domain-joined Windows device to Entra. It is not the same as Intune enrollment or compliance. Read the proposed policy grant: requiring compliance still requires a compliant device even when it is hybrid joined.
No computer management requirement leaves those computers out of the planned device requirement. Other applicable Conditional Access policies still apply.
Saving a choice changes the plan. It does not enroll a device or configure Intune.

limits: Direct Send and connector-based SMTP relay do not sign in with user accounts, so these logs do not inventory them. A legacy-authentication block targets password-based sign-ins, not every mail-sending device. Confirm the sending method and test important jobs with their owners.
Authentication that happens outside Entra (federation, third-party MFA, on-premises apps) is recorded as a sign-in but not as what the other system enforced.
Anything on a longer cycle than the records (the quarterly invoice run, the yearly renewal) has left no evidence yet; keep new blocks in report-only across a full cycle.
Credentials saved on equipment nobody has touched in years surface the day something blocks them; a walk through the comms room beats any report.
A partner's own tenant enforces for their people; IAMAI sees their sign-ins here, never their controls.

home.metaTitle: IAMAI — Microsoft Entra Conditional Access planner
home.metaDescription: Check who could be affected by your Microsoft Entra security changes. IAMAI reviews your tenant and helps you plan the work before you deploy.
home.h1: Know what needs attention before you change a policy.
home.siteLine: A policy can look right and still cause problems. IAMAI checks who has the required sign-in methods, whether the available records show they use them, and which exclusions or outside accounts need a closer look. Then it helps you plan the changes.
heroMeta: You review and make the changes
home.workHeading: See what needs doing, and what needs to happen first.
home.workLead: Start with the tenant you have. IAMAI compares it with your chosen baseline, shows the gaps it can assess, and puts the work in order.

work.text: Review policies, accounts, groups and the sign-in evidence Microsoft makes available to this tenant.
See what already meets the baseline, what needs attention, and who a change could affect.
Work through the prerequisites, review the instructions, and test changes before enforcing them.

home.baseline: The default is Defense in Depth: Conditional Access policies, built by Jon Hope, a Microsoft MVP.
home.baselineGoal: It covers MFA, administrator access, devices, sessions and more. IAMAI helps you work through the parts that apply to your tenant and prepare for changes that could affect people’s access.
home.baselineNote: You can inspect the baseline version IAMAI uses or load your own. Where IAMAI cannot assess a control, the plan identifies the review you need to carry out.
home.catchesHeading: A few things worth checking before you deploy.

catches.text: Guests may need different preparation or follow-up before a change applies to them.

home.trustLabel: What it does with your tenant
home.trustHeading: Your tenant stays under your control.

trust.title: IAMAI does not change your tenant
trust.body: You can review the permissions before connecting. IAMAI reads the tenant to build the plan; you decide which changes to make and carry them out yourself.

trust.title: Your scan is processed on your device
trust.body: Tenant data is read from Microsoft and processed in your browser. IAMAI does not upload your scan to its own server. Downloaded plans and copied briefings can contain tenant information, so review them before sharing. The website host may also collect page-load information.

trust.title: You can inspect the code
trust.body: The source and documented limits are public. Check how IAMAI works, report a problem, or suggest an improvement.

home.about: I’m Lachlan Robinette. I work with Microsoft Entra security baselines across MSP-managed tenants. I built IAMAI to help with the checks and decisions that sit between a baseline and a successful rollout. It is still in public preview. If something is wrong or unclear, tell me at feedback@getiamai.com.

plan.needsScan: Nothing to plan until the first scan.
plan.exclusionsGroupRailSub: Select the group containing your emergency accounts for policy exclusions.
plan.jsonWaits: {steps} first: this policy names an object {tenant} does not have yet.
plan.jsonWaitsDecision: Baseline mappings first (Plan settings): the baseline names a group of its author's, and IAMAI does not yet know whether it stands for something in {tenant} or is left out.
plan.jsonWaitsUnreadable: The source policy leaves out a group IAMAI cannot identify, so a copy made in {tenant} would reach people the author's own tenant left alone.
plan.inPlaceKeep: This is in place already: nothing to create. Keep the policy as it is.
plan.pairReviewExpected: Expected policy name: {name}. Confirm its scope and authentication requirement before assigning this name to an existing policy. Rescan after making an approved correction.
plan.pairUnmatched: IAMAI found existing guest coverage in {tenant}, but cannot match it to the two baseline policies. Compare the existing policies with the expected pair before creating or renaming anything. See Entra for the names to check.
plan.targetAmbiguous: {tenant} has more than one policy this goal could correct, and nothing about them says which is its own. IAMAI does not guess: correcting the wrong one would change who another policy applies to. Decide which policy stands for this goal (for example, widen it to everyone, or retire the extra one), then scan again.
plan.noOperation: This step has no policy for IAMAI to write in this plan. Scan {tenant} again to rebuild it.
plan.manualCorrection: IAMAI does not write this change: the policy is not what the plan asked for in {fields}. Correct it in the Entra admin center, then scan {tenant} again.
plan.emergencyUnsafe: This policy would apply to {tenant}'s emergency access accounts. IAMAI writes nothing until the exclusions group carves them out: fix the exclusions-group step, then scan again.
plan.emergencyUnproven: IAMAI cannot prove this policy leaves {tenant}'s emergency access accounts out of scope, because it could not read who is in the group the policy excludes. Nothing is offered on a reading that did not finish: scan again.
plan.escapeHatchHeld: Running this would turn the policy on straight away, and the way back in to {tenant} is not verified yet. Finish {steps} first; the instructions come back when its checks pass.
plan.readinessHeld: Running this would change what {tenant}'s people have to do straight away, and {measure} is {value} - this step waits until it reaches {threshold}. The instructions come back when it does.

stepContract.$comment: The Step Contract (Foundation D, src/ui/surfaces/stepContract.ts). Every Plan step answers the same questions in the same order: where it is now and what happens next, why, what IAMAI found, who it touches, what to do, what to fix first, how you will know it is done, and More. These are the words the contract itself supplies; each step's own sentences stay in its steps[] entry.

kind.$comment: The opened step's eyebrow (task 034; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html draws `Policy step` and `Resolution step` above the title). One label per steps[].kind, so the label names what production already calls the step rather than a second taxonomy. A kind with no entry here shows no eyebrow.

stepContract.$commentRailExisting: The In-place variant's own side block (task 036; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html V4 draws `Existing implementation` over the policy's name). The name is Step.satisfiedBy — the coverage result that decided the goal was satisfied — so the rail names the tenant's own policy and never the baseline's. `railExistingKeep` is the sub under one sufficient policy; `railExistingTogether` is the sub where two cover the goal between them and neither covers it alone.
stepContract.railExistingKeep: Nothing to create; keep it as it is.
stepContract.railExistingTogether: Together — neither covers the goal on its own.

railChannels.$comment: The rail's Implementation block as the approved Plan pack draws a side block (task 035; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html `.side-list`): one short item per channel rather than one sentence naming all three. It restates `implementationReady` in the pack's grammar and adds no fact — the channels stand or fall together on Foundation A's one answer (roadmap/operations.ts implementationOffered), so a step that offers none shows `implementationNone` instead and no list at all.

foundLabel.$comment: The key over each finding card (task 035; docs/design/approved/plan-step-v1.html `.finding .k`). It names which KIND of finding this is — the classification stepContract.ts foundOf already makes when it builds the list — and never restates the finding's own sentence.

stepContract.whoUnknown: IAMAI cannot establish exactly who this reaches: this scan could not settle the policy's scope, so no count is shown.
stepContract.whoUnknownDecision: IAMAI cannot establish who this reaches until the baseline's references are mapped in Plan settings, so no count is shown.

stateWords.$comment: The Plan state words the one projection adds (src/ui/surfaces/planState.ts): a policy the tenant already enforces that the plan must change and cannot yet, and emergency access whose minimum is in place while its hardening is deferred to Cleanup.

stepContract.foundReadiness: Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}; it is {value} today.
stepContract.foundReadinessFloor: Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}. At least {value} are ready: {line}
stepContract.$commentFoundReadinessUnmeasured: A threshold against a non-number is a dead end: "waits for MFA readiness to reach 90%; it is not measured today" told three times on one step, with nothing saying WHAT could not be measured or what would move it. The count is computed (roadmap/methodReadiness.ts) and was rendered nowhere.
stepContract.foundReadinessUnmeasured: Enforcement waits for {measure} to reach {threshold}. It is not measured yet: {line}
stepContract.foundEnforcedShort: This policy is enforced, and {line} Anyone it does not accept is refused where it applies until they register a method it does.

readinessScope.$comment: Who a readiness measure counts, by its family (copy/reasons.ts READINESS_MEASURE), in the enforced policy's informational threshold sentence (U22).

readinessRoute.$comment: Where a readiness number is moved, by its family (copy/reasons.ts READINESS_MEASURE), for a measure the plan itself has no step for. A family with no entry states the number alone.
readinessRoute.device: Device readiness moves in Intune, not here: enroll the devices on the chosen platforms and assign a compliance policy, then scan again. No step of this plan enrolls a device for you.

stepContract.$commentFoundReadinessRouteStep: A gate that says what it waits for but not what opens it is half a sentence. The plan already knows: generate.ts draws the edge from a readiness-held step to the campaign that moves the number, and the step it drew to was named nowhere on the held step. Only where that edge exists.
stepContract.foundReadinessRouteStep: The step that moves this number is “{step}”.

readinessValue.$comment: The threshold tile's collapsed value, by its measure's family (copy/reasons.ts READINESS_MEASURE): the percentage and what it measures (content review S3). A family with no entry shows the percentage alone.
readinessValue.device: {value} of people on a compliant device

stepContract.foundInPlace: {tenant} already has a policy doing this, so there is nothing to create.
stepContract.foundInPlaceNamed: Already delivered by {policies}, so there is nothing to create.
stepContract.$commentFoundShortfall: A goal can be delivered and still miss most of the directory. coverage.ts records who it does not reach and why, for every goal, and the sentence never reached a surface: a policy excluding a group that holds 116 of 122 accounts read "already delivered, so there is nothing to create" beside "6 active people", with nothing naming the gap.
stepContract.foundShortfall: This goal is written for {active} people in this tenant; {n} of them are excluded from the policy that delivers it, so it reaches {reached}.
stepContract.$commentFoundWider: A step named for one group offering to create a policy that reaches everybody. "Require MFA for Guests", on a tenant with one guest, offered the baseline's tenant-wide MFA policy under a name that promised guests: follow it and you apply MFA to the whole company from a step named for one guest. Disclosure, not substitution — two Foundation A invariants say the goal's population must never decide which policy is built, and they are right.
stepContract.foundWider: This step is named for {cohort}, and the policy it would create applies to everyone in the tenant. That is the baseline source IAMAI matched to this goal, and it is not narrowed to {cohort}. Read its assignments before you create it.

foundWiderCohort.$comment: The cohort a step is named for, by the goal's expectedWho kind (data/goals.json). Only the kinds for which a tenant-wide policy is a real widening appear: members is mapped to one by the baseline author on purpose.

stepContract.$commentFoundDiffers: The deployed policy is not what this step asked for, in a part IAMAI writes. The comparison existed and its answer was discarded after deciding readiness, so a policy built with a narrowing condition left at Configure: No — the trap the step's own procedure warns about — rendered identically to one built exactly right.
stepContract.foundDiffers: {policy} is deployed, but not as this step asked: {fields} differ from the target above. Compare them in the Entra admin center, or re-run this step's instructions to write the intended settings.
stepContract.$commentFoundWatched: A step IAMAI WATCHED move is not a report of coverage that was already there (stepContract.ts foundOf, observation.ts since === 'observed-change'). Saying "already delivered ... so there is nothing to create" on the step somebody has just created, watched for a week and enforced erases their work and describes it as a policy they never needed to build.
stepContract.foundInPlaceWatched: {policies} is in place. IAMAI watched it get there.
stepContract.foundInPlaceWatchedTogether: {policies} are in place together, and no one of them covers the whole goal on its own. IAMAI watched them get there.
stepContract.foundInPlaceTogether: Already delivered by {policies} together — none of them covers the whole goal on its own — so there is nothing to create.
stepContract.doneSatisfied: The scan found the assessed configuration in place.
stepContract.doneConflict: The baseline author publishes a version that resolves the contradiction between the policy's documentation and its definition.
stepContract.doneDecision: The question on this step is answered and saved.
stepContract.doneMissing: Every object this policy names exists in {tenant}.
stepContract.doneMissingDecision: Every group of the author's this policy names has an answer: what stands for it in {tenant}, or none needed.
stepContract.doneMissingUnreadable: IAMAI can say what the group the source policy leaves out means for {tenant}.
stepContract.donePair: Both guest policies are enabled with the intended settings, and representative guest sign-ins meet the required MFA method. Resolving the policy names is preparation for that work.
stepContract.doneTarget: One policy in {tenant} stands out as this goal's own, and a scan finds it.
stepContract.doneEscapeHatch: {steps} passes its checks, so the way back in to {tenant} is verified.
stepContract.doneEmergency: Every emergency access account is provably out of scope of this policy.
stepContract.doneOperation: A scan rebuilds this step with a policy IAMAI can write.
stepContract.doneManual: The policy holds what the plan asked for in {fields}.
stepContract.doneVerify: You have looked at the accounts this step names and dealt with them.
stepContract.doneDeploy: The policy exists in {tenant} in report-only.
stepContract.setAsideAction: Put this step back if you want it on the plan again.
stepContract.$commentFixStepAt: A prerequisite is not always waited on until it is FINISHED (src/actionability/dependency-data.json carries the milestone on every edge). Turn Off Security Defaults waits for the replacement policies to be ready to enforce; those policies wait for it to be complete. Both tiles said "Finish the other first", so the pair read as a deadlock that the data does not contain — and the way out of an apparent deadlock is to turn security defaults off, which is the one thing the step's own words say not to do yet.

fixStepAt.ready-to-enforce: {step} needs to be ready to enforce first — not finished, just ready.
fixStepAt.minimum-satisfied: {step} needs its minimum safety checks passed first.
fixStepAt.hardening-complete: {step} needs its hardening cleared or deferred first.
fixStepAt.recovery-verified: {step} needs a verified recovery test first.

stepContract.fixConfirmExclusions: Complete {step} first. IAMAI found a matching group, but needs your confirmation before this policy can reference it.
stepContract.fixMapping: Map the baseline's reference under Plan settings, Baseline mappings, or leave it out there.
stepContract.fixReview: {name} is no longer the policy IAMAI was watching: find out what changed on it, and why, before it goes any further.
stepContract.doneReview: What changed on the policy is accounted for, and a later scan finds it is still the policy IAMAI is watching.
stepContract.doneSetAside: Nothing is expected of this step while it is deferred.

headings.$comment: The section titles the Plan draws a step with, in the order the contract states them. One source: the opened step, the Cleanup rows and the review page all read these, so a heading cannot say one thing on one surface and another somewhere else.

stepContract.attentionConflict: Do not deploy this policy from the current baseline

hardening.$comment: Emergency access in two tiers (owner, 2026-09-11; validation/emergencyTiers.ts): the minimum safety checks are Readiness tiles and hold the rollout; the resilience hardening is its own Readiness tile, which the operator may defer to Cleanup.
hardening.heading: Hardening recommendations
hardening.leadBlocked: These make emergency access more resilient. Clear the other Readiness items first; these can then be fixed or deferred.
hardening.leadDefer: Minimum emergency access is available, but less resilient than recommended. Fix these, or defer them: the rollout continues, and they stay in Cleanup until they pass.
hardening.deferredOn: Deferred to Cleanup on {date}. The rollout continues, and these stay in Cleanup until they pass.
hardening.unchecked: {n} more could not be checked on this scan.
hardening.doneDeferred: Minimum emergency access is in place; the deferred hardening stays in Cleanup until it passes.

tiles.$comment: One Readiness tile per emergency account slot (B10 P0-7, S-BG-1): labelled by the selected account's name, or Account 1 / Account 2 while nobody is selected for it.
tiles.notSelectedNote: Choose an emergency access account in the action column, then save.

readiness.$comment: The opened step's Readiness region (docs/design/approved/anatomy/plan-step-v1.html `.readiness-strip` / `.readiness-bar`, owner update Sep 10, 2026). Tile labels, short values and the bar's headline only: every note and every sub-line is an existing sentence the contract already carries (stepContract.ts readinessOf), so nothing here states a fact of its own.
readiness.heading: Readiness

tiles.decisionFound: IAMAI found {group}. Confirm this is the right group.
tiles.exclusionsReachNote: The count shows policies this scan verified. Selecting the group does not change a policy; each policy step adds it where it is missing.
tiles.peopleNote: This is the population IAMAI resolved for this policy. It is not a prediction that every account will be prompted.
tiles.observationNote: Review the available records and the remaining evidence requirements. Time elapsed alone does not complete this check.
tiles.observationDateNote: This is the earliest review date, not a scheduled automatic enforcement.
tiles.coverageNote: IAMAI found an existing control that meets the assessed goal. Keep it unless a separate reviewed change is needed.
tiles.peopleStepNote: These are the accounts this step asks you to review. Check the listed evidence before deciding what each account needs.
tiles.$commentCoverageUnreadable: A goal an existing policy already delivers reads In place / Completed, and said nothing about whether the people it covers can actually satisfy it. On a tenant whose registration source returned 403 the step read Completed beside a readiness of "0 of 40 people have a registered method allowed by the target policies. Method compatibility is not yet established for 40" - which the engine had computed and the completed step did not show. In place describes the policy; it is not a finding about the people, and a reader takes Completed as protection.
tiles.coverageUnreadable: IAMAI could not read whether the people it covers can satisfy it: {line} This describes the policy, not the people.
tiles.$commentAwaitingReview: A policy that is enforced and waiting on the person to record their workflow test rendered Ready / Enforced, milestone Review now, and ZERO readiness tiles and ZERO findings - three readers reported the same empty step, two of them on the same step id. Its Done-when listed five lines: three that IAMAI checks itself and two that are the person, with nothing saying which of them remained. The step knows: awaitsWorkflowRecord is true and manualReview.confirmedAt is not set.
tiles.awaitingReviewNote: The policy is enforced and IAMAI is finished with it. What is left is yours to record: test the workflows below and confirm the outcome on this step.

bar.$comment: The readiness bar's headline by the Ready lane's substatus (A1b): the other lanes read their own label, the blocker label or the tenant fact (stepContract.ts readinessOf).

results.$comment: A package readiness gate's result as its tile value (stepPackage.ts mergeReadiness). The protocol's words (protocol.ts READINESS_RESULTS) stay the package's; the page says these, so the retired Blocked never renders (B11 P1-7).

implementation.$comment: The opened step's Implementation region (docs/design/approved/anatomy/plan-step-v1.html `.implementation-section`). The channels are production's own artifacts — the portal translator, stepPowerShell.ts, stepJson.ts and the step context the prompts read (roadmap/prompts.ts stepContext) — and `empty` is the one truthful no-action box a step shows when it offers none of them, by the reason it offers none.
implementation.heading: Implementation
implementation.aiWarning: Contains tenant context. Review before sharing with an external AI service.

aiFacts.$comment: The briefing every AI Info carries (stepBody.ts, aiGrounding.ts): the shared opening, the package's own words for the state, then IAMAI's facts for the step in six sections, so an assistant needs no screen. Observations, saved choices, proposals and unknowns are kept apart; never confirmation that a change was made.
aiFacts.heading: IAMAI FACTS FOR THIS STEP
aiFacts.boundary: What follows is what IAMAI observed in this tenant's latest scan and what its plan proposes. It does not confirm that any change has been made.
aiFacts.members: Policies IAMAI tracks for this step
aiFacts.existing: Tenant policies already delivering this goal
aiFacts.changedFields: Fields that differ from the target
aiFacts.target: Names and IDs in the intended target
aiFacts.more: {n} more accounts are not included in this excerpt.
opening: Help me understand and carry out this IAMAI step. Explain its purpose, who it affects, how the tenant's observed state compares with the intended result, and what remains to do. Use the facts below; distinguish observations, saved decisions, proposed changes and unknowns.

Explain the next available action first, then the settings and checks needed to complete it. Point out any conflict between the instructions and the supplied policy data. If Microsoft behavior needs clarification, use current Microsoft documentation and cite the relevant page. Do not invent tenant values, approvals, completed checks or changes. Ask only for information that affects the next action.

You may explain alternatives and their tradeoffs. Clearly identify any alternative that changes the selected baseline or saved decision, and do not present it as the current plan. Do not execute a tenant change from this briefing.
aiFacts.proposed: IAMAI proposes these settings. The step cannot hand them over yet; What remains says why.
aiFacts.previewValues: Values shown as ‹…› are not resolved yet. Do not run this output.

implementation.excludeUsersNone: none: the resolved target excludes no individual accounts
implementation.channelUnavailable: This format has no output for the current action. Use the available guidance and readiness checks on this step.

inPlace: The tenant already delivers this, so nothing is generated for it.
observe: No tenant change to submit right now
The policy stays in report-only while IAMAI observes it.
decision: Answer the question this step is waiting on first.
unavailable: No artifact for this policy yet
IAMAI offers no artifact for this policy as it stands.
conflict: Not enough information to provide implementation guidance.
The baseline defines this policy two ways. Until the baseline author publishes a corrected version, no implementation steps are available.
none: This step describes no policy for IAMAI to generate.
bindingMissing: IAMAI does not yet hold every value this change needs, so no artifact is produced.
confirmationsPending: IAMAI cannot read these from Microsoft. Confirm them under Readiness, and the enforcement artifacts appear here.
packageFault: This step's implementation content could not be projected safely, so no artifact is offered.
correctionUnknown: IAMAI found a difference on this policy that the step’s corrections do not cover, so no partial correction is offered.

preview.$comment: The planning preview (owner, 2026-09-11): a step whose implementation is authored but not yet executable shows the work with no Copy (stepPackage.ts planningPreview). No Planned work banner is drawn over it (U4); these lines are what B5 puts on the disabled Copy.
preview.text: You can copy this guidance. Resolve the prerequisites and any missing values before applying the change.
preview.textValues: You can copy this draft. Fill in the unresolved values and review the result before running it.
preview.checks: Checks to confirm first are under Readiness.

review.$comment: A package the semantic re-pin review sets aside (src/content/implementation/drift.ts): the step draws the baseline's own channels instead.
review.reviewNeeded: IAMAI's written guidance for this step was reviewed against an earlier version of its baseline policy, which has changed since. Until it is reviewed again, these steps come from the baseline itself.
review.held: A baseline policy this step's written guidance was reviewed for is no longer in the baseline, so that guidance is not shown.

values.$comment: What an unresolved package binding is called inside a planning preview. A binding with no entry here is named from its own key.
values.account.decision.disposition: what to do with the account
values.admin.peopleToSeparate: admins who need a separate admin account
values.mfa.perUser.accounts: accounts still on legacy account-level MFA
values.policies.unmanagedBrowser.a.target.sessi: first unmanaged browser policy session controls
values.policies.unmanagedBrowser.b.target.sessi: second unmanaged browser policy session controls
values.policy.target.conditionsWithExclusion: policy conditions with the exclusions group

implementation.powershellInvocation: Defines the script and runs it in {modes} mode with IAMAI's values

passkey.$comment: The passkey settings step in words (roadmap/passkeySettings.ts, owner approval 2026-09-14): what the scan read, the change IAMAI resolved from it, and why no change is offered where it cannot be built without overwriting something. Bound into the passkey package as passkey.current.summary, passkey.target.summary and passkey.review.detail.
passkey.current: Passkey (FIDO2) is {state}. Key restrictions: {restriction}. Attestation: {attestation}. Self-service registration: {selfService}. Included: {includes}. Excluded: {excludes}.

target.unrestricted: Keep key restrictions off, so every model that can register today still can, including Microsoft Authenticator.
target.allow: Keep the allow list and its existing allowed models ({retained}); add approved authenticator models ({added}).
target.allowPresent: Keep the allow list and its existing allowed models ({retained}); the required authenticator models are already allowed.
target.block: Keep the block list as it is ({blocked}); it does not block Microsoft Authenticator.
target.common: Enable the method and self-service registration, require attestation for new registrations, and keep the target groups and exclusions shown in the resolved configuration.

review.profiles: This tenant uses passkey profiles. IAMAI does not read profile settings, so it cannot tell which groups can use Microsoft Authenticator passkeys. Review each profile and its group assignments in the Entra admin center and keep them unchanged; IAMAI does not write the older global settings over a profile-based policy.
review.blockListConflict: The key restriction block list blocks Microsoft Authenticator ({aaguids}). IAMAI does not remove a block list entry. Find out why it was blocked before allowing Authenticator passkeys.
review.partialRead: The scan did not return every passkey setting this change is built from ({fields}). IAMAI cannot build an update that preserves the current configuration, so none is offered.

workloadIdentity.$comment: The workload (Cloud Sync) step in words (roadmap/workloadIdentity.ts, owner-approved methodology 2026-09-14): why a network restriction is not counted as protection for the sync process. Bound into the workload package as workload.identity.detail.
workloadIdentity.unknown: IAMAI has not established that this identity supports workload Conditional Access. Confirm support before relying on the proposed restriction.
workloadIdentity.unsupported: This identity type is outside Microsoft's supported scope for workload Conditional Access. This policy cannot be counted as verified protection for the sync process.

implementation.copyFailed: Copy failed. Select the text and copy it manually.

railTransition.$comment: The rail's sub-line under a day the plan schedules (roadmap/stepSchedule.ts transition): what that day is for. Preparation, verification and review read the milestone's own words instead.

rollout.$comment: The footer's rollout exception (docs/design/approved/anatomy/plan-step-v1.html `#rollout-dialog`). It is the existing skip (roadmap/sets.ts): the step leaves the rollout with the operator's reason recorded, and it never counts as implemented.
rollout.title: Defer this step
rollout.body: A deferred step remains recorded as an exception. It does not count as implemented or as satisfying the baseline.
rollout.placeholder: Record why this step is being deferred.

troubleshooting.$comment: The labels a package troubleshooting scenario is drawn under (authoring guide v2.5 §30.3). Every scenario itself is the package author's (docs/implementation-content/<step-id>/CONTENT.md troubleshooting.model).

confirm.$comment: A person's confirmation of a check IAMAI cannot read from Microsoft (an implementation-content package's human-validation prerequisite). Opened from the Readiness tile that states the check; the tile's own line is the package author's.
confirm.body: IAMAI cannot read this from Microsoft. Confirm it only once you have checked it yourself: the confirmation stays with this plan until what it was given against changes.

stepContract.fixCompletedReference: {step} is complete, but this policy still has an unresolved reference. Confirm its tenant object under Baseline mappings, then rescan.

plan.mfaReadinessHold: {n} people are not yet confirmed ready for this sign-in requirement. Review whether they need setup, recent proof, or a successful evidence read.

mfaReadinessHoldUnknown.$comment: Where the scan could not work out who a step's readiness hold reaches (MfaHandoff.tsx), by the hold's family: the line before the link, the link, and any words after it (content review S3).
mfaReadinessHoldUnknown.mfa: This scan could not work out who cannot meet this step's sign-in requirement yet.
mfaReadinessHoldUnknown.guest: This scan could not work out who cannot meet this step's sign-in requirement yet.
mfaReadinessHoldUnknown.admin: Check which admins don't have a phishing-resistant method yet:

mfaPreview.$comment: The Plan step's preview of the people its own gate names (prompt 62): worded in the step's own requirement, never MFA Readiness's higher bar.
mfaPreview.higherBar: MFA Readiness holds the higher bar: phishing-resistant on every device.

plan.recoveryTestAccounts: I tested recovery with these accounts:
plan.manualReviewExplain: IAMAI cannot verify the whole review. Confirm only after you have met the completion criteria above. Changes to the reviewed accounts or settings may reopen this step.
plan.manualReviewScanFirst: Complete the changes above and scan again. The account or setting checks must pass before you can record this review.

workflows.title: Confirm the Services You Use
workflows.why: Your plan should cover the services this tenant uses. Activity helps IAMAI find them, but a quiet service may still need protection.
workflows.instructions: Review these services. Services found in use are selected for your confirmation. Add anything the scan missed; leave uncertain answers as Not sure.
workflows.done: You have confirmed which listed services are in use.
workflows.notUsed: You confirmed that {service} is not in use.
workflows.reviewWhy: Check the baseline's control for {service} against the way this tenant really uses it, before deciding whether it belongs here.
workflows.source: Baseline reference: {policy}. Open View Baseline Definition below to inspect the original settings.
workflows.generic: Identify what the policy protects, who it includes and excludes, and which access requirements it applies.
reviewInstructions: Match every application, group, location and authentication strength in the baseline to the intended object in this tenant. Never reuse a baseline author’s tenant-specific IDs.
Check the policies already here, and exclude the emergency access accounts from anything that blocks or restricts sign-in. A report-only policy blocks nobody and needs no exclusion.
Create it in report-only, leave it there for a week, and read the sign-in logs before you turn it on.
Test the exclusions as well as the rule: another policy can still ask an excluded person for MFA.
To back a change out, disable the policy rather than delete it; a deleted one can be restored for 30 days and no longer.
Confirm that the intended access works and unwanted access is blocked. Record the review below only after you have validated the control; IAMAI does not verify completion of this manual step.
workflows.reviewDone: You have reviewed the policy for this tenant, made any necessary changes, and tested the intended access and restrictions. IAMAI holds that record against the version you read, and asks again when the policy or the objects it names change.

policies.title: Review SharePoint and OneDrive Access outside Trusted Locations
policies.why: Check whether files should be accessible away from your trusted networks, including the effect on remote workers.
instructions: Review the baseline’s SharePoint and OneDrive block policy. Confirm the trusted locations and the people or groups it exempts before deciding how it should apply here.

policies.title: Review MFA for Inforcer Access
policies.why: If this tenant uses Inforcer, confirm that its sign-ins receive the MFA protection you intend.
instructions: Review the Inforcer application targeted by the baseline and confirm it is the enterprise application used by this tenant. Check the included and excluded groups and whether an existing policy already requires MFA for the same sign-ins.

policies.title: Review Who Can Use Azure Virtual Desktop
policies.why: Only the people intended to use virtual desktops should be able to sign in to them.
instructions: Review the AVD block policy and the group allowed to use it. Confirm the AVD application and the group that should be allowed through; a wrong exception can block legitimate desktop access.

policies.title: Review Where Azure Virtual Desktop Can Be Used
policies.why: Confirm whether virtual desktop access should be limited to trusted networks.
instructions: Review the AVD application block outside trusted locations. Confirm the network definitions and exemptions against how people connect to their desktops.

policies.title: Review MFA for the Baseline’s Azure Application Scope
policies.why: Confirm that the Azure application scope receives the intended authentication requirement without disrupting legitimate administration.

On a 4,900-person tenant it read 3 where 2,339 people were on registered computers, and this question decides whether every company computer gets joined and enrolled: at 3 that is a Tuesday afternoon, at 2,339 it is a change board and a pilot. plan.$commentNoOperationDisabled: "This step has no policy for IAMAI to write in this plan. Scan again to rebuild it." was said over a step whose policy EXISTS in the tenant and is switched off - the step was tracking it, state disabled, on both the latest scan and the one before. So the sentence was false and its remedy did nothing: a reader scanned three times, got byte-identical output, and stopped. Said where every policy this step tracks is disabled.
plan.noOperationDisabled: A policy for this step already exists in {tenant} and is switched off, so there is nothing for IAMAI to create. Turning it on is a change in the Entra admin center; if it has not been watched in Report-only, set it there first. Scan again once it is on.
plan.$commentEnforceOutstanding: The enforce checklist is headed "Do not turn it on unless all of these are true now" and lists three conditions, authored identically in forty-odd packages. It never carried the step own unresolved prerequisites - so a tenant with security defaults still ON had a tile reading "Turn Off Security Defaults - Prerequisite - Waiting" four lines above a checklist that did not mention them, on a policy the security-defaults step names as one of its four replacements. Eight policies were enforced into a state the product itself calls unsupported and irreversible. Spliced into the list rather than authored per package, so every package gets it and none can be missed.

plan.$commentSecurityDefaultsCoexist: The plan states its own ordering invariant on this step - "security defaults must be off before the policies replacing them can take over, and once these policies exist you cannot turn security defaults back on... That is why nothing in this plan enforces before this step." A reader enforced eight policies with security defaults still on, swept all thirty-three steps, and found no warning anywhere; the board read Completed and the tile said "IAMAI watched it get there." The step that owns the invariant is the one place that must notice it has been broken.

alerting.title: Alert on Emergency Account Sign-ins
alerting.why: An alert is how anyone finds out an emergency account was used. It also tells a planned drill apart from access nobody expected.
whatToDo: Send the sign-in logs somewhere they can be queried first: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Monitoring & health → Diagnostic settings → + Add diagnostic setting, pick the sign-in categories, then Send to Log Analytics workspace. That takes at least the Security Administrator role, an Azure subscription and a workspace — or the SIEM you already use.
The accounts are {list:emergencyAccountUpns}. Take each one's object ID from Entra ID → Users; the rule matches on the object ID, not the sign-in name, because a name can be changed under it.

In the Azure portal, as at least a Monitoring Contributor: Monitor → Alerts → + Create → Alert rule. Scope: the workspace. Condition: Signal name Custom log search, Query type Aggregated logs, a SigninLogs query filtered to those object IDs. Alert logic: Static, Greater than, threshold 0.
Give it an action group that reaches a person by email, SMS, push or voice, set Severity 0 - Critical, enable it on creation, and name who answers it.
Test it with one controlled sign-in and confirm the alert arrives. Agree what the responder then does: keep the logs, and decide whether the use was a drill, a real emergency, or neither.
Review ingestion, retention and cost for the monitoring service you use.
doneWhen: A controlled sign-in by an emergency account produced an alert at the monitored destination, and the response owner confirmed receipt.
The response owner knows what happens next: keep the logs, then decide whether the use was a drill, a real emergency, or neither.

hardening.title: Harden Emergency Access
hardening.why: These emergency-access checks were deferred once the minimum ones passed. This is the Cleanup row a scan can close for you: each deferred check has to pass again on the tenant.
whatToDo: {list:hardening}
Do each one, then scan again: the row closes when they pass. A deferral was a decision to wait, never a result, so nothing here counts as done until the scan finds it.
doneWhen: Every deferred emergency access recommendation passes on a scan.

namedExclusions.title: Remove Emergency Accounts Excluded by Name
namedExclusions.why: These policies leave an emergency account out by name as well as through the exclusions group. IAMAI keeps exclusions your tenant already has, so its corrections leave these names in place. The exclusions group should be the only way an emergency account is left out: one group is easier to check and keep right than names spread across policies.
whatToDo: Remove the emergency accounts named under Users → Exclude in {list:namedExclusions}
Before you remove a name, check that the exclusions group holds that account and that the policy excludes the group. The group is what keeps the account out once its name is gone. Then scan again.
doneWhen: A scan finds no On or Report-only policy that excludes an emergency account by name, and the exclusions group keeps each account out.

naming.title: Align Policy Names
naming.why: A naming standard lets the next person find a policy and understand its purpose without opening it. That is what makes the review after this one possible.
whatToDo: Rename {list:renames}
A name that carries its own meaning has a sequence number, the resources it applies to, the response, who it applies to and when. IAMAI proposes names in the convention this tenant already uses.
A Conditional Access policy has no owner field, so put ownership in the name — a team prefix will do — and keep a register elsewhere of who answers for each one.
Renaming changes no Conditional Access evaluation, but scripts or reports that find policies by name may need updating; keep the same policy IDs and settings.
doneWhen: The reviewed policies use the approved names on the next scan.
Verify after the change: tooling that finds these policies still identifies them.

consolidation.title: Review Overlapping Policies
consolidation.why: A tenant is capped at 240 Conditional Access policies, the ones that are off included, so an overlap costs something. It also makes the next change harder to reason about.
whatToDo: Compare the complete settings of {list:overlaps}: scope, exclusions, conditions, controls, risk levels and guest types.

Choose Retain Both and record why when the policies serve different requirements. Otherwise select and save the retained policy and the policies to retire below before disabling or deleting anything. After the approved retirement, scan again so IAMAI can verify the retained policy is enforced and the retired policies are disabled or absent.
Retire by disabling, not deleting: a disabled policy comes back with one switch, while a deleted one can be restored for 30 days and no longer.

Retire a policy only after the remaining one is shown to preserve the required coverage, tested and approved; keep a rollback record. Never remove High-risk coverage because a Medium-only policy exists.
doneWhen: Each overlap has been reviewed: retain both with a recorded reason, or verify the retired policy has a tested replacement preserving its required coverage.

steps.title: Prepare Emergency Access Accounts
steps.why: Prepare at least two dedicated emergency access accounts with approved passkeys. These provide administrative access when your normal sign-in is unavailable. Two accounts give you another recovery option if one account or its passkey cannot be used.

who.operatorNote: Use these accounts only for emergency recovery and controlled tests. Do not use them for daily administration.

decision.label: Emergency access accounts
decision.help: Select the accounts dedicated to emergency access, then save.

whatToDo.lead: Select the accounts dedicated to emergency access, then save.
create: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → New user → Create new user.
Enter a unique username, such as emergency-access-primary or emergency-access-secondary, or choose another account name. Select the observed initial domain from the domain list.
Keep the account cloud-only and enabled, then assign Global Administrator through the applicable direct-assignment or PIM route.
Store the initial password securely where authorized staff can retrieve it without signing in to this tenant.
Register an approved passkey, scan again, select the new account and Save.

lockedOut.label: If a change locks you out
steps: Sign in with one of the emergency accounts above, in a private browser window.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Conditional Access → Policies → open the policy that changed today → Enable policy: Report-only (or Off) → Save. It applies within minutes.

If the portal itself is blocked: sign in from a device and network the policies trust (a managed laptop on the office network), or from any device run Connect-MgGraph -Scopes Policy.ReadWrite.ConditionalAccess and then Update-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy -ConditionalAccessPolicyId <id> -State enabledForReportingButNotEnforced.
If no route works, Microsoft support can help; they will ask for the tenant id: {tenantId}.

steps.title: Disable or Confirm Dormant Accounts
steps.why: Unused accounts can leave access behind after a person or service stops needing it. IAMAI lists an account with no successful sign-in for 90 days; Microsoft calls 90 to 180 a reasonable window. A blank record is not proof of disuse: the directory keeps sign-ins only so far back, and never fills the gap in later.

who.licenceNote: Last sign-in dates need Entra ID P1; without it this scan cannot tell a dormant account from one in daily use, so it lists none and the review is yours.

whatToDo.lead: Review each account with its owner and record the outcome.
steps: Disable it: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → the account → Edit properties → Account enabled: No. Keep the mailbox if anything still needs it.
Or confirm it is in use and have the owner sign in; the directory's record can take a day to catch up.
Or, if it is a shared mailbox or a resource that should never sign in, block sign-in the same way; it then stays listed under Inventory and nowhere else.

steps.why: User risk is Microsoft's reading of the account rather than one sign-in: how likely it is that the account itself is compromised. Most of that reading is worked out after a sign-in, so this policy is what stops a compromised account the next time it is used.

evidence: {n} people had a sign-in rated high risk since {from}: {list:riskyUsers}
Identity Protection's risky users report is a separate surface this plan does not read, so the people it holds may not be the people named here.
The baseline asks for risk remediation with {strengthName}, which lets Microsoft pick the remediation each person's registered methods allow.
A person has to be registered for multifactor authentication before this policy reaches them; without it they are blocked and somebody has to reset the account by hand.
A synchronized account needs the on-premises password route enabled before its owner can remediate.
Check how the policy treats guests rated high risk: they cannot remediate in this tenant, because their risk is held in their home directory.
{existingCoverage}

before: Synchronized users who remediate with a password change need password writeback in Entra Connect.
A synchronized user who changes the password on-premises instead needs password hash synchronization and the on-premises password-change setting that clears user risk.
Check that people in scope have a registered multifactor authentication method; remediation asks for it first, and this is not the self-service password reset flow.

steps.doneEnd: An account {tenant} rates high risk cannot be used again until its owner has completed the remediation the baseline's authentication strength accepts, and the exclusions group is applied.
doneWhen: A scan confirms the high-risk user policy is On with the intended recovery controls and exclusions.
People rated at risk were reviewed. Affected users can complete the required remediation, including the on-premises password route where their account is synchronized.

risks.text: A person with no registered multifactor authentication method cannot complete remediation at all and needs an administrator to reset the account.

A guest or external account this policy reaches is blocked rather than remediated: the password it would have to change is held in the account's home directory, and nobody here can clear the risk for it.

helpDesk: Someone stuck in a password-change loop: reset the account for them. Completing the remediation clears the risk by itself, so nothing has to be dismissed by hand afterwards.
A guest reporting a block: their risk and their password both live in their home directory. There is nothing to reset or dismiss in this tenant.
more.manager: When Microsoft rates an account high risk, the person is asked to complete remediation at the next sign-in instead of waiting for someone to read a report.

example.sspr: it is enabled for all users

Name: {policyName}

Target resources → Resources → All resources
Conditions → User risk → Configure: Yes, then High
Grant → Require risk remediation with Require authentication strength: {strengthName}; Require all the selected controls. Session → Sign-in frequency → Every time
{reportOnlyLine}

steps.aiFocus: Explain adaptive remediation rather than a universal password reset. Separate SSPR recovery, MFA readiness, the hybrid password routes and external-user support.

steps.title: Challenge Medium-Risk Sign-ins
steps.why: A medium rating means Microsoft saw one or more moderate anomalies in the sign-in and is less confident than it is at high. This rule asks for multifactor authentication at that level, and leaves the High-risk rule its own stronger requirement.

evidence: A separate response from Challenge High-Risk Sign-ins: Medium-risk sign-ins get built-in MFA, and the High-risk policy keeps its own requirement.
{n} sign-ins were rated medium risk since {from}: {list:mediumRiskUsers}
The baseline asks for multifactor authentication here, not the authentication strength the High-risk policy uses, and it adds no session control.
{existingCoverage}

steps.doneEnd: A sign-in {tenant} rates medium risk cannot continue until it is answered with multifactor authentication, and the exclusions group is applied.
doneWhen: A scan confirms the medium-risk sign-in policy is On and requires the intended MFA controls for the intended users, with the correct exclusions.

risks.text: Travel and new devices trigger prompts more often; that is expected.
A person with no registered method is blocked rather than prompted, and this policy stops them registering one during the risky sign-in.

helpDesk: Repeated prompts after travel: answering the prompt clears the sign-in risk by itself, so there is nothing to dismiss afterwards.
A sign-in blocked with AADSTS53004: the person has no registered method, and cannot register one while the sign-in is risky.
more.manager: Sign-ins Microsoft rates medium risk need MFA before they continue; sign-ins outside that rating are not affected by this policy.

steps: {portalRoot}
Name: {policyName}
Users → Include: All users. {exclusionsLine}
Target resources → Resources → All resources
Conditions → Sign-in risk → Configure: Yes, then Medium
Grant → Require multifactor authentication. No session control: the baseline sets none here
{reportOnlyLine}

steps.aiFocus: Keep sign-in risk separate from user risk, and Medium separate from High. Do not add a session control from generic guidance to this retained target.

steps.title: Reset Passwords for Medium-Risk Users
steps.why: A medium rating means Microsoft saw moderate anomalies on the account and is less confident than it is at high. This rule answers that with the baseline's authentication strength and a secure password change, and leaves the separate High-risk control in place.

evidence: This policy covers Medium user risk only. Keep the separate High-risk control unless a reviewed replacement preserves that coverage.
{n} people had a sign-in rated medium risk or higher since {from}: {list:mediumRiskUsers}
The baseline asks for {strengthName} and a password change together here, and adds no session control.
People in scope need a registered MFA method to complete the secure password change; synchronized users also need password writeback.
Guests and external accounts are excluded from this policy, because the password they would have to change is held in their home directory.
{existingCoverage}

before: Synchronized users who change their password here need password writeback in Entra Connect.
Check that people in scope have a registered MFA method; the secure password change asks for it first.
verification: Verify the MFA and secure password-change recovery path for the account types in scope, including password writeback where synchronized users require it.
Record a controlled recovery test with its account type, path, date and result. Keep the separate High user-risk protection in place.

steps.doneEnd: An account {tenant} rates medium risk cannot be used again until its owner has answered the baseline's authentication strength and changed the password, and the exclusions group is applied.
doneWhen: {policyDoneWhen}
People in scope can complete MFA and the secure password change, and the High user-risk policy remains in place.

risks.text: More people are asked to change passwords than with the high-only policy; each change is a few minutes.

helpDesk: Check the sign-in failure and the Medium-risk policy’s actual recovery requirement. Help the person complete the supported secure password-change or administrator recovery process, then verify the risk and sign-in result. Investigate the detection before dismissing risk.
more.manager: When Microsoft rates an account medium risk, the person completes MFA and a secure password change at the next sign-in. The separate High-risk policy stays in place.

example.sspr: it is enabled for all users

Target resources → Resources → All resources

{reportOnlyLine}

steps.title: Use Separate Accounts for Admin Work
steps.why: Personal email is phished constantly, so the account that opens mail should not also hold a directory role. Move the role to an account that does nothing else, and test it before taking access off the everyday one.

who.lead: Review the {n} administrator accounts for dedicated administration.
evidence: Recent mail or Teams activity: {list:adminsWithWorkload}
who.licenceNote: Mail and Teams activity needs Entra ID P1; without it IAMAI sees no everyday use here, and the review is yours.

whatToDo.lead: Review active and eligible administrator accounts. If they are already dedicated to admin work, record that outcome. Otherwise test a dedicated replacement before removing everyday access.
steps: Create a second, cloud-only account for the role, named so the purpose is obvious (adm- and their name).
Give it no mailbox to read, but an email address that reaches the person: role approvals and service notices still have to arrive.
Register a passkey or security key on the admin account before its first use; the admin policies require one.

Assign the role to the admin account under the same governance model, keeping PIM eligibility where the everyday account used it: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Roles and administrators → the role → Add assignment.
Sign in with the admin account and complete the admin task it needs; only then remove the role from the everyday account.
Keep mail, Teams and files on the everyday account; open admin portals with the admin account only.

doneWhen: The reviewed privileged accounts are confirmed as dedicated to administrator work, or each recorded handover has a tested replacement with the required roles and the everyday account no longer has privileged roles.
Mailbox licensing and past mail or Teams activity are clues for the review; their absence does not prove separation.
steps.ifWrong: Put the role back on the everyday account; nothing else changes.

risks.text: An admin who keeps doing admin work from the everyday account never sees the separation; moving the role is what makes it real.
Two marks Microsoft gives for this review: fewer than five Global Administrators, and fewer than ten privileged role assignments in all.

helpDesk: An admin refused by a portal on the everyday account: the role moved; sign in with the admin account.
more.manager: Admin work moves to accounts that do nothing else, so a phished mailbox is not a phished tenant. Without this, every admin inbox is a way in to every setting.

steps.aiFocus: Distinguish direct roles from PIM and keep the staged handover. Historical mail or Teams events do not mean a completed migration failed.

steps.title: Restrict Service Accounts to the Trusted Network
steps.why: Restricting user-based service accounts to approved networks can reduce where their passwords are useful. Review all job locations so an infrequent or vendor-hosted process is not missed.

who.none: No service accounts recognised in {tenant}; nothing for this policy to restrict.
evidence: {existingCoverage}

steps.doneEnd: The user-based service accounts in the group can sign in to {tenant} only from the approved trusted network, and every job that uses one has been run from there and recorded.
doneWhen: {policyDoneWhen}
Each required job works from its expected network, including scheduled and infrequent ones.

risks.text: A user-based service job outside the approved trusted locations can stop when this policy is enforced. Confirm the execution network and test scheduled or infrequent jobs.
A trusted network that lists a whole ISP range trusts every customer on it.

helpDesk: Inspect the failed job's account, sign-in result and public egress address. Confirm whether the job belongs on an already approved network; adding a new trusted network changes every policy that relies on that trust.
more.manager: Service accounts in the group can sign in only from the approved trusted network, which limits where their passwords are useful. A call made by a service principal is not blocked by a policy scoped to users; covering one takes Conditional Access for workload identities, which Restrict the Directory Sync Service Principal to Its Address builds.

example.policyName: Core - Block - Service accounts outside the trusted network

steps: {portalRoot}
Name: {policyName}
Users → Include: Groups: {serviceAccountsGroup}. {exclusionsLine}
Target resources → Resources → All resources
Network (formerly Conditions → Locations) → Configure: Yes, then Include: Any network or location; Exclude: {trustedLocation}
Grant → Block access
{reportOnlyLine}

steps.aiFocus: Include the user-account group and actual workflow evidence. Do not infer service-principal protection or approve a network from sign-in history alone.

verification: Identify each required job, its user-based service account and public egress network. Run a controlled test from the approved location, including jobs that run infrequently.
Confirm the intended policy applies and the job succeeds. Record the account, job/network, date and outcome; an interactive sign-in is not a substitute for the actual job.

whatToDo.lead: Security defaults provide Microsoft's default identity protections on this licence. Check the requirements first, then turn them on if this is the chosen approach.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Overview → Properties → Manage security defaults.
Enabled → Save.
Tell people they may be asked to set up an authentication method, and give anyone who cannot a way to reach IT support.

doneWhen: The scan reports Security Defaults enabled. Registration readiness is tracked in its own step.
steps.aiFocus: Explain the selected protection model and observed setup gaps. Do not confuse enabling Security Defaults with customizing Conditional Access.

whatToDo.lead: Find what still authenticates the old way, so blocking it later does not break a needed service.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Monitoring & health → Sign-in logs, and add the Client app column.
Filter the records you have (up to 30 days) to legacy clients: Exchange ActiveSync, IMAP, POP, SMTP, Other clients.
For every account that appears, find the application behind it and its owner, and ask owners about jobs that run only occasionally.
Record a supported replacement or retirement for each, and test it before blocking access.

doneWhen: The available sign-in records show no successful legacy-client sign-in, or every one left has a named owner and a recorded replacement or outstanding action.
steps.aiFocus: Report the actual evidence window and unresolved dependencies. Do not claim thirty days of coverage when the records do not contain it.

comms.body: Please identify each application, printer or scheduled job that signs in with an older client or username-and-password protocol. Include its account, actual protocol, owner, normal and infrequent run schedules, supported replacement and a delivery or access test window.

whatToDo.lead: App passwords let older applications sign in without an interactive MFA check. Replace each dependency before retiring the credential.
steps: Ask users and application owners which applications still use app passwords, and migrate or retire those applications before removing their credentials.

In Entra admin center, open Entra ID → Users → Multifactor authentication. Select the affected users, open Manage user settings, select Delete all existing app passwords generated by the selected users, then save. Use an authorized Authentication Administrator or Authentication Policy Administrator account.
Separately open the per-user MFA service settings through Conditional Access → Named locations → Configure MFA trusted IPs. Clear the option allowing users to create app passwords, then save.
Disabling creation does not delete existing app passwords. Record the reviewed accounts and the removal and creation-setting checks below.

doneWhen: The reviewed applications no longer depend on app passwords, and the affected app passwords are removed.
Creating new app passwords is disabled where that applies.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish per-user credentials from tenant method-policy settings. Do not invent a complete app-password inventory from unavailable data.

comms.body: We are retiring app passwords. Please identify any application or job that uses one, arrange its supported replacement and test access with us before removing the credential. Confirm the old app password has been removed and report any failed workflow so we can finish the change.

whatToDo.lead: Keep MFA enforced while you move it from the per-user setting to the replacement you choose.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies → Manage migration → Migration in progress.
Under Policies, enable every method people actually use, so nobody loses the one they have.
Confirm the replacement MFA protection is enabled and covers each account before changing that account's per-user MFA state.
Entra admin center → Entra ID → Users → Per-user MFA: set an account to Disabled only once its replacement protection is in place; keep the existing setting where no replacement exists.
Manage migration → Migration complete.

doneWhen: The tenant reports Migration complete, and no account is left Enabled or Enforced for per-user MFA.
Every account whose per-user MFA was disabled is covered by enabled replacement protection.
steps.aiFocus: Explain why a completed methods migration is not permission to disable every user's MFA state.

whatToDo.lead: Global Administrator has broad authority. Keep it only where the work needs it.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Roles & admins → Global Administrator: list active and eligible holders and why each needs the role.
Where a narrower role is enough, assign and test it before removing Global Administrator.
Keep the selected emergency accounts; they are counted here and they are the way back in.
Record the reason for each retained assignment.

doneWhen: Every active and eligible Global Administrator assignment has a recorded purpose, and unnecessary access has been removed while preserving the selected emergency accounts.
The recommended number of administrators is a review aid; a count alone does not prove least privilege.
steps.aiFocus: Treat counts as review signals, not proof. Separate emergency accounts, eligible access and day-to-day administration.

whatToDo.lead: Review guest access with the people who sponsor it, so access that is no longer needed ends through the proper process.
steps: Entra admin center → Identity → Users, filter User type to Guest, and add the Creation time and Last sign-in columns.
For each guest, confirm the sponsor and whether the work still needs the access.
Check pending invitations with whoever sent them; a pending invitation is not automatically obsolete.
Remove access that is no longer needed through your organization's offboarding and retention process.

doneWhen: Every reviewed guest or invitation has a confirmed purpose, or an approved removal that has been completed.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish pending, inactive and unsupported evidence. Do not infer approval to delete from a missing sponsor field.

whatToDo.lead: Move people from text and voice codes to a stronger approved method, and test it before retiring the old one.
steps: Entra admin center → Entra ID → Authentication methods → Policies: enable the approved replacement method (Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys) for the intended users.
Help people on text message or voice call register the replacement and complete a successful sign-in with it.
Review recovery needs and application dependencies, then disable Text message and Voice call through the approved method-policy change.

doneWhen: Text message and voice call are off in the authentication methods policy, and everyone who used them has registered Authenticator or a passkey.
Each of them signed in with the replacement, and the agreed recovery path is preserved.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish stronger MFA from phishing-resistant MFA. Do not claim all Authenticator modes are phishing-resistant.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the trusted location's reported problems: every policy that uses it depends on its ranges. Check the enabled policies that use it before saving, then verify the intended traffic and rescan.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the trusted location passes on the next scan.
Its ranges match the approved decision.
steps.aiFocus: Explain the failed check, affected location and dependent policies. Trust does not mean every sign-in requirement is bypassed.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the allowed-countries findings: the list decides where the countries policy allows sign-ins. Review the dependent enabled policies before saving, and rescan afterward.
steps: Open Entra admin center, then Conditional Access, then Named locations. Select the location used by your country restriction policy.
Compare its country list with the approved countries shown in this plan. Review policies already using the location before saving a change, because enabled policies use the new list immediately.
Correct the findings shown on this step, then scan again to check the result.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the allowed-countries list passes on the next scan.
The named location matches the approved country decision.
steps.aiFocus: Separate approved scope, observed geography and unresolved travel needs.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the pilot group's findings: it decides who tests a new control first, so its members should represent the work the change affects.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the pilot group passes on the next scan.
The pilot membership is the approved one.
steps.aiFocus: Explain why each membership or scope issue matters without implying a pilot guarantees a safe wider rollout.

whatToDo.lead: Resolve the service-account findings with each workload owner: a wrong classification can interrupt a job or leave an ordinary account outside important controls.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the service accounts passes on the next scan.
The confirmed service-account decisions are reflected in the plan.
steps.aiFocus: Distinguish user-based service accounts from workload identities and explain the actual affected policies.

whatToDo.lead: Correct the authentication strength's reported differences: it is the list of methods its policies accept. Review every policy that references it, keep the same object where supported, then verify and rescan.

doneWhen: Every must-fix check on the authentication strength passes on the next scan.
The strength has the intended combinations.
steps.aiFocus: Include the current and intended combinations, affected policies and TAP where present.

steps.title: Keep Company Data Off Phones
steps.why: You said company data does not belong on phones, so a policy of your own has to say no to them: leaving iOS and Android out of the managed-device rule only means that rule never asks them anything. A Conditional Access policy that includes those two platforms and blocks access is the rule that says no.

who.lead: People who access company resources from iOS or Android.

whatToDo.lead: Implement and test the phone access restriction before marking this review complete.
steps: Entra admin center → Conditional Access → Policies → New policy. Name it for what it does, so the next person reading the list can see it.
Users → Include: All users. Exclude → Groups: the emergency exclusions group. Never exclude an emergency account by name.
Target resources → Resources → All resources.
Conditions → Device platforms: set Configure to Yes, then Include: Android and iOS. Left at No the condition applies to every platform, and Block access there would lock out every computer as well.
Grant → Block access.
Enable policy: Report-only, then read the report-only results for a working week. They name the people and the apps this would have stopped, which is who will call.
Test from a real iPhone and a real Android phone, in a work app and in the browser, and check that recovery and administrator access still work from a computer. Then enable the policy.
Record the policy, its scope and the test result in your change record. Confirm this step only when the restriction is enforced and the tests pass.

doneWhen: iOS and Android are blocked by a policy of this tenant's own, the affected access paths have been tested, and you have recorded the result.

risks.text: The platform is what the client reports about itself, in the user agent string, and Microsoft does not verify it. A phone whose browser claims to be a computer is not stopped by this policy.
This blocks a phone from signing in. It is not a data-loss control: company data already on a phone, and any route that does not go through Microsoft Entra sign-in, are untouched.
Everyone loses phone access, including the people on call. Agree the exception route — a laptop, or a named exclusion — before the policy is enabled, not after the first call.

helpDesk: A person blocked on their phone: confirm the sign-in shows iOS or Android, and answer with the agreed route rather than widening the policy.
Microsoft's own guidance is that the device-platform condition belongs either with Intune compliance or in a block statement. This is the block statement.
more.manager: Phones cannot reach company accounts at all, which is what the device answer asked for. Anyone who needs access away from a desk needs a computer or an agreed exception.

steps.aiFocus: Explain the difference between leaving phones out of a compliance requirement and actively blocking access. Help the administrator scope and test the restriction without changing baseline policies or emergency access blindly.

steps.title: Require MFA for Inforcer Access
steps.why: A token for Inforcer needs MFA, whichever app asks for it: Conditional Access follows the resource, not the client. One policy therefore covers every route people take into the application.

evidence: Inforcer application ID: 708861da-226e-4d65-a57a-24128df64524.
{existingCoverage}

doneWhen: {policyDoneWhen}
The intended user can access Inforcer with an accepted MFA method.

comms.body: We are reviewing MFA protection for Inforcer access. Please register an approved MFA method for your work account and contact IT if sign-in fails or you need help testing access. Tell IT about any unattended job using a person’s account.

risks.text: A policy scoped to users never reaches a service principal calling Inforcer; a workload identity needs a policy of its own.
One policy per application adds up: a tenant is capped at 240, and Microsoft prefers one policy covering all resources.

helpDesk: Inspect the affected Inforcer sign-in and its Conditional Access result. Check the target application ID, user scope, exclusions and accepted MFA claim.
more.manager: Inforcer user sign-ins require MFA through the app-specific policy.

Name: {policyName}
Users → All users. {exclusionsLine}
Target resources → Inforcer (application ID 708861da-226e-4d65-a57a-24128df64524).
Grant → Require multifactor authentication
{reportOnlyLine}
